channel_name: Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy
video_title: She Knows the 250 People Building AI. Here's What They Actually Believe.
gist: Sarah, founder of the early-stage AI firm Conviction (Harvey, Chai Discovery, Sunday Robotics, Base 10), maps what the roughly 250 people actually pushing the AI frontier now believe: a violently and globally competitive landscape, a newly widespread belief that recursive self-improvement puts exponential intelligence one-to-two years out, and a creeping sense among lab researchers that only compute scale matters. She argues the binding constraints are physical and political — energy, data-center siting, supply-chain concentration and public consent — not technical, and lays out a technology-forward underwriting process (model-capability fit first, memos, 1-10 instinct ratings, 4-6 new companies a week) plus newly-flipped convictions on semis, biology and open-source models as the real diffusion channel for AI into the economy.

themes.theme: Investing an AI cycle with no back-test

insights.claim: Investors deploying into AI in 2026 have no historical back-test for the regime, leaving them stuck between missing the opportunity and repeating the mistake of every prior technology boom-bust.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Position sizing, not stock selection, is the live decision for AI-exposed portfolios; a manager who cannot articulate which side of that trade-off they are taking is taking it by default.
insights.quote: do you miss the opportunity on one side or, you know, do you make the mistake of every boom bus cycle in technology history?

insights.claim: A senior investor described the current posture toward AI risk to Sarah as wanting to brake hard while still accelerating, capturing an industry that is fully aware it may be in a bubble and is deploying anyway.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Self-aware capital is still capital — awareness of froth is not producing discipline, so expect valuations to keep clearing above fundamentals until an exogenous shock forces the brake.
insights.quote: I keep saying I want to press the brakes as hard as I can but I'm not doing it I'm going 90 miles an hour

insights.claim: Sarah is explicitly long AI and is positioning her firm against a monolithic outcome in which one to three frontier-model owners consume the economy, a future she says she does not want and does not expect.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: The bet is that value accrues broadly across applications, infrastructure and open models rather than concentrating in two or three labs — the opposite of the 'labs eat everything' trade.
insights.quote: the owner of one, two, three frontier models consumes the economy. I do not want that future

insights.claim: Sarah subscribes to a great-person theory of technology outcomes: whether a competitive Western open-source model exists in five years depends on whether specific individuals raised the capital, gathered the talent and committed to fight for the frontier.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Treat structural forecasts about AI market structure as contingent on identifiable founders and funding decisions, not as inevitabilities — the outcome is still purchasable.

insights.claim: The most dangerous behavior Sarah sees in the current AI funding environment is investors proxying judgment to founder pedigree and referral quality while having no fundamental intuition for the technical bet itself.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A leading indicator of loss concentration: rounds priced entirely on pedigree signals will mark down hardest when the research theses fail to compound.
insights.quote: it's not all going to work

insights.claim: Because frontier research founders are pitching capex-heavy bets to capital allocators who are not research scientists, storytelling quality and making the bet legible has become a genuine determinant of which research companies get funded.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Expect funding outcomes among technically comparable research startups to diverge on narrative skill — an exploitable inefficiency for investors who can underwrite the science directly.

themes.theme: What the ~250 frontier builders actually believe

insights.claim: Conviction organizes its firm strategy around a defined set of roughly 250 entrepreneurs and researchers whom it considers the people actually pushing the AI frontier forward, aiming to know and support all of them.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A concentrated-relationship model rather than a deal-volume model — the competitive moat is coverage of a small, nameable population, which is replicable by other firms willing to narrow scope.
insights.quote: there's sort of 250ish people that he thinks about

insights.claim: The defining change in the frontier AI community over the past 12 months is that competition has become violently and globally competitive to a degree materially beyond 24 and 36 months ago, with insecurity because the global dimension breaks the prevailing narrative.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Competitive intensity is compressing model release cycles and raising talent costs; assume shorter durability for any single lab's capability lead.
insights.quote: It is a violently competitive landscape.

insights.claim: Within the last 12 months a large share of frontier researchers newly adopted the belief that recursive self-improvement — AI research models improving the models themselves — puts some form of exponential intelligence one to two years away.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: This belief, not revenue, is what justifies current capex and talent pricing at the labs; watch for it breaking, because the spending case unwinds with it.
insights.quote: with recursive self-improvement of AI research models that can improve the models themselves we are a year two years away from uh some sort of exponential intelligence

insights.claim: Sarah flags the two-year-to-AGI belief as suspect by citing Andre Karpathy's self-aware admission that he has believed superintelligence was two years away for roughly ten years — and believes it again now.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Discount timeline claims from insiders as structurally biased; the same people have been persistently early, which argues for underwriting AI businesses on today's capabilities rather than a two-year step-change.
insights.quote: I've thought it was two years away for about 10 years

insights.claim: The scale of the major labs — thousands of employees and compute budgets discussed at the $750 billion level — has broken the individual researcher's sense of contribution, versus an earlier era when a 200-person lab meant every person moved the needle.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Diminished ownership at scale is a talent-retention risk for the big labs and a formation catalyst for research spinouts — a supply of high-quality startups for early-stage investors.

insights.claim: Two disempowering beliefs are spreading among lab researchers: that their own work does not matter because the model will do it, or that the only thing that matters is compute scale.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: If frontier researchers themselves believe capital, not ideas, is the binding input, the marginal value of research talent falls relative to the marginal value of compute and energy assets.
insights.quote: the only thing that matters is compute scale

insights.claim: Sarah does not believe every researcher doing frontier work at the top couple of labs currently feels essential to the machine.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Watch for accelerating senior-researcher departures from the largest labs into smaller, higher-agency ventures — the source of the next cohort of frontier startups.
insights.quote: I don't think every researcher um doing frontier work at these top couple labs right now feels like they're essential to the machine

insights.claim: Conviction underwrites application markets technology-forward — asking which workflows and professions are a good fit for the models' capabilities — rather than working exclusively backward from the customer problem, which Sarah acknowledges most investors consider nonsense.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A repeatable screen: rank professions by structural fit to current model capabilities to find the next Harvey-shaped opportunity before customer demand is legible.

insights.claim: The Harvey thesis came from recognizing in late 2022 that law is structured language — heavy document reading, abundant precedent text inside firms and in common law, and text generation — making it a near-perfect match for next-token prediction plus retrieval.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: The template generalizes: any profession whose output is structured language over a large precedent corpus is a candidate for the same capability-fit trade.
insights.quote: law is structured language

insights.claim: What sold Sarah on Harvey's founders Winston and Gabe was the ambition of the leap they were underwriting — from answering a question about a California landlord-tenant agreement to doing 85% of the work on an Activision Blizzard-scale M&A.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Underwrite the size of the founder's projected capability leap alongside the technical logic — the ambition gap, not the demo, was the differentiating signal.

insights.claim: Sarah is instinctive on people, typically landing at an 8 or 9 on an internal 1-10 scale within the first meeting, then spends the following days-to-weeks hunting for the holes in her own understanding rather than building conviction upward.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A falsification-first process: the diligence question is 'what would move me', which is more transferable than the more common climb-to-conviction approach.
insights.quote: I'm like okay I'm like immediately an eight or a nine

insights.claim: Sarah writes a full Greylock-style memo on every deal — she did so even when the firm was just her — and ships it to outside investors like John Lily or Dylan Field for a second read outside the fund.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: An external-critic loop deliberately built outside the partnership's incentives — cheap to copy and a check on internal deal momentum.

insights.claim: Sarah will not hold an 8-or-9 rating on a company whose underlying science she does not understand, and treats investing without grounded intuition in the bet as the core failure mode of the current period.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A discipline test for allocators: if a manager cannot explain the technical theory of a position beyond the founder's résumé, the position is unowned risk.
insights.quote: can you really be an eight or a nine if you don't get it? Like, no.

insights.claim: Sarah argues that founder quality and idea quality are inextricable — she cannot assess someone's judgment without understanding what they are doing — which limits the pure back-the-person exception she'd grant to someone like Brett Taylor.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Cuts against the 'back the founder, ignore the idea' heuristic that dominates in hot markets; judgment is only observable inside a domain you can evaluate.

insights.claim: Conviction assigns single-person ownership of every investment decision; Sarah calls a peer firm's no-individual-ownership model nonsense because somebody has to own the decision.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Accountable decision rights are a diligence question for LPs evaluating emerging managers — consensus-vote firms diffuse both credit and error attribution.
insights.quote: somebody has to own the decision

insights.claim: Sarah now sees only four to six new companies a week, versus roughly 500 in her first couple of months at her prior firm, having traded volume for calibration.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for deal-flow discipline: elite early-stage output is now coming from very low volume plus deep pre-existing relationships, not funnel breadth.
insights.quote: I probably see four to six new companies a week

insights.claim: Sarah spends roughly two-thirds of her time on portfolio company work — recruiting, helping founders think, influencing the outside ecosystem — with fundraising next and evaluating new companies only third.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Time allocation reveals where the firm believes its returns are made: post-investment support and ecosystem position, not sourcing throughput.
insights.quote: I think I spend 2/3s of my time working on portfolio company stuff

insights.claim: Sarah deliberately spends learning time with public-markets investors and other asset classes, and with incumbents such as a pharma company rethinking its business around AI, to avoid the myopia of a purely early-stage ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Cross-asset-class information flow is a stated sourcing edge — incumbents' AI beliefs are early evidence of where enterprise budgets will move.

insights.claim: Sarah considers constructing grand strategic frameworks about which layer of the AI stack will win to be a waste of investing energy, and instead evaluates each lab priority — ChatGPT, ads, coding, co-work expansion — against each specific company or opportunity.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Argues against the dominant 'thin wrapper vs platform' debate consuming investor attention; competitive risk is assessed per-company against a specific lab roadmap instead.
insights.quote: coming up with some grand strategic framework for like what layer is going to win here I think is not useful to me

insights.claim: Sarah directs her analytical energy at the diffusion question — if AI is 1% deployed, what does the next 99% look like — rather than at frontier-lab strategy.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Points the opportunity set at deployment, integration and inference economics rather than model training — where most of the remaining value creation sits if she is right.
insights.quote: if we're 1% of the way in, what is the next 99% of diffusion?

insights.claim: Sarah passed on investing in Mikey Schulman's music-generation company because she doubted how many people want to make music, and now cites it as evidence she systematically underestimated demand for AI-driven expression, entertainment and creation.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A named blind spot at a top AI investor: consumer creative AI demand is being underwritten too conservatively, which implies persistent mispricing in that category.
insights.quote: I don't think that many people want to make music. I make music, right?

themes.theme: Compute independence and the physical bottleneck

insights.claim: An infrastructure leader at one of the hyperscalers told Sarah that nothing will move the needle for them at sufficient scale before 2030, and AI infrastructure planning conversations now routinely reference 2032.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Anchors the energy-constraint horizon: any AI capacity thesis resolving before 2030 depends on existing gas and grid, not new build — bullish for incumbent generation and interconnect-adjacent assets.
insights.quote: there was nothing that is going to move the needle for us at sufficient scale before 2030

insights.claim: Sarah argues the constraint on abundant cheap energy for data centers is regulatory and public-consent alignment, not technical or entrepreneurial capability — you must convince New Yorkers to want data centers and convince the public that nuclear is safe before the cost curve can come down.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Makes permitting, siting and public opinion the highest-leverage variables in AI infrastructure returns — screen power projects on political feasibility over engineering.
insights.quote: I don't think we lack the technical and entrepreneurial capability to build abundant cheap energy for the data centers

insights.claim: Physical supply chain build-out — tacit knowledge, skilled labor and raw materials — is structurally unable to move at software or decision-making speed, and Sarah says the only route is sustained investment through it.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Sets a hard floor on AI buildout timelines and argues for durable pricing power in scarce physical execution capability — the opposite of software's marginal-cost dynamics.

insights.claim: Sarah expects compute independence to become a major policy and investment topic, framing it as analogous to energy independence with thin-sieve chokepoints — she cites TSMC directly — that sit in places not necessarily stable or accessible to the US and allies.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A forming policy narrative to trade ahead of: supply-chain redundancy spending across fabs, components and materials, similar in shape to the energy independence buildout.
insights.quote: I think we're going to start talking much more about compute independence

insights.claim: Jacob Hellberg is working on an effort called PACIA to map every part of the compute supply chain and identify where additional capacity and independent paths can be built; Sarah stresses the goal is more than one source rather than full US onshoring, because comparative advantage is real.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Redundancy, not reshoring, is the likely policy shape — favors second-source suppliers and allied-country capacity over pure domestic-content plays.

insights.claim: Conviction has invested against the compute buildout in the data-center labor gap and robotics, nuclear energy, and alternative chip architectures, but has repeatedly declined data-center builders and solar/battery installers because those are financing-and-operations businesses without a durable product asset.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A clean line for the AI infrastructure trade: venture capital is chasing the technology layers while the operational buildout, dominated by financing, is being left to other capital pools.

insights.claim: Sarah argues there is no version of the world in which the US rebuilds its industrial base without automation, because the country will not import labor, domestic labor is expensive, and Americans do not want and should not want $13-an-hour inhuman jobs.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Ties the reshoring policy agenda directly to robotics and automation demand — the political commitment to domestic manufacturing is implicitly a commitment to buying robots.
insights.quote: people in the United States do not want to work and should not want to work for $13 an hour doing a very inhuman job

insights.claim: Sarah's central political risk scenario is that rational public fear of AI job losses plus resentment at rent capture by a small number of technology firms fuses into an anti-capitalist coalition that slows energy, infrastructure and compute buildout, leaving the US non-competitive.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: The main tail risk to the AI capex thesis is political rather than technical or financial — monitor public opinion and local siting fights as leading indicators.

themes.theme: Open-source models as the diffusion channel

insights.claim: Sarah's view on competitive open-source models is that the cat is out of the bag: over the past three years increasingly competitive open models have come from China but also the US and Europe, including work from Thinky, Poolside, Reflection and Nvidia.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Any thesis premised on closed frontier models capturing all inference value is already outdated; Western open-weight supply is arriving from multiple funded efforts.
insights.quote: the cat is out of the bag

insights.claim: A large number of real-world AI use cases are too expensive, too sensitive or too slow to run on today's frontier providers, and Sarah expects that share to grow as the economy learns to do more with AI because inference is genuinely expensive.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Structural demand for open-weight models and independent inference providers grows with adoption rather than shrinking — a durable tailwind for the serving layer.
insights.quote: There are a huge number of instances where it is too expensive, too sensitive or too slow to use the like model from the frontier providers today.

insights.claim: Restricting open-source model use in the United States would only restrict law-abiding American businesses, slow them down and shift profits, while adversarial actors would be unaffected by those restrictions.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: The industry's core lobbying argument against open-weight restrictions; if it loses, expect a compliance drag on US AI adopters without a corresponding security gain.
insights.quote: you'd basically just restrict law-abiding American businesses

insights.claim: Sarah's preferred policy response to fears of backdoored Chinese models is rigorous frontier safety testing rather than speculation, noting that concern about backdoor behaviors currently far outruns the actual research done on it.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Identifies model-evaluation and safety-testing capacity as an under-supplied function that policy demand is likely to fund.

insights.claim: Sarah accepts the dual-use symmetry directly: frontier capability that works for defensive cybersecurity and biology work necessarily also works for offensive cyber and biosecurity misuse, so the safety profile must be tracked as capability progresses.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Dual-use risk is conceded even by open-source advocates, meaning controls will land somewhere — likely on deployment and monitoring rather than on model weights.

insights.claim: Sarah argues frontier lab researchers cannot possibly imagine the diversity of real-world use cases, so broad access to intelligence too cheap to meter has to be delivered through an ecosystem of businesses using open models, post-training skills, harnesses and cheap infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: The economic case for the application and tooling layer: value creation scales with the number of independent actors adapting models, not with lab headcount.

insights.claim: Sarah says it is entirely possible the US ends up without abundant low-cost intelligence in a competitive way, drawing the parallel to the alternate history in which the US built a thousand reactors and had energy too cheap to meter but did not.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Cheap abundant intelligence is treated as a policy choice rather than a technological inevitability — the nuclear analogy is the base rate for how such choices can go wrong.

themes.theme: Re-underwriting hostile markets: semis, biology, robotics

insights.claim: Conviction's internal debates rarely concern the direction of technological travel and almost always concern whether a given market is friendly to a venture-backed company — space being the example of a market that is unfriendly but still possible.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Separates technology risk from market-structure risk explicitly; the second is what actually kills returns in hard-tech categories.

insights.claim: Venture investing in semiconductor companies was historically a god-awful business, but Conviction now believes the risk equation has changed because of consolidated at-scale demand for accelerators and because large buyers themselves want supply-chain independence.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A named regime change in an asset class most VCs wrote off; buyer-funded second-sourcing is the mechanism that makes new chip companies financeable.
insights.quote: was like a god-awful business for the longest time

insights.claim: Sarah has moved from uncertainty to a strong yes on the thesis that models can create and capture enormous value in biology, based on empirical data from the portfolio rather than a priori reasoning.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: One of the few explicit belief-updates in the conversation, and it points capital toward AI-for-biology software rather than traditional therapeutics structures.
insights.quote: I'm a strong yes now

insights.claim: Conviction wrote the first check into Chai Discovery, which is now working with a number of top-10 pharma companies to accelerate parts of the R&D process, with a $10 million contract cited as concrete validation.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Hard evidence that large pharma will pay software-scale contracts for AI R&D tools — the revenue proof point the 'you can't sell software to pharma' consensus said wouldn't exist.

insights.claim: The conventional wisdom Sarah is betting against holds that the only way to make money serving pharma is to make a drug, with traditional biotech firms assembling companies around principal investigators and owning 40% — a structure she believes models now make unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: If correct, it opens a software-margin, software-ownership path into pharma value that neither biotech VCs nor software VCs have historically been positioned for.

insights.claim: Sarah identifies the industry's forthcoming light-bulb moment as the first new indication or drug whose trajectory was clearly changed by AI, which she expects will trigger a huge wave of investment.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A specific, observable catalyst to front-run: position in AI-for-biology before the first credible AI-attributed clinical asset re-rates the whole category.
insights.quote: I think we should see a massive acceleration in cures

insights.claim: Sarah is surprised by how fast pharma and healthcare overall have accepted that AI will make a difference and change their business, contradicting the sector's reputation for slow adoption.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI budget expansion in healthcare may arrive earlier than models assume — relevant to vendors selling into pharma R&D.

insights.claim: Sarah credits Sunday Robotics founders Tony and Chang — young Stanford PhD students with backgrounds at Toyota Research, DeepMind and Tesla — with contributing most of the interesting ideas in robotics AI over the last four years.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Concentration of robotics research output in very few young people is a talent-scarcity signal — the founding team is the scarce asset, not the technology.
insights.quote: I think that they have contributed dualhandedly more most of the interesting ideas in robotics AI over the last four years

insights.claim: The binding constraint in robotics is the absence of an internet-scale robotics dataset, so the key research problem is cheap data collection that still covers the distribution of real-world environments and tasks — the problem Sunday Robotics attacks.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Screen robotics investments on data-acquisition strategy and cost per environment rather than on model or hardware claims — that is where the generalization problem is actually solved.

insights.claim: Sunday Robotics, under two years old, expects general semi-humanoid robots doing tasks in people's homes in beta by the end of this year, having built the full stack, manufactured domestically, with hundreds of hardware iterations.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable milestone that runs ahead of the robotics consensus of 'when, not if' — a near-term test of whether home robotics timelines have genuinely compressed.
insights.quote: this entire team believes that we are going to have general semihumanoid robot thoughts doing things in people's homes like first in beta end of this year

insights.claim: Sarah thinks gaming and entertainment will be totally different because of AI and that investors are super under-exposed to it.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: An explicitly under-owned category flagged by a top AI investor — the same blind spot she admits caused her to pass on AI music generation.
insights.quote: gaming and entertainment is going to be like totally different and people are um you know super underexed on it

themes.theme: Building a firm and the LP bargain

insights.claim: Sarah's edge thesis at founding was that firm growth and generational transitions had made early-stage less competitive than usual precisely as a massive technology transition arrived, so focus plus first-principles technical understanding would buy better access and better decisions.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: The stated alpha was structural and time-limited; as competitors re-tool around AI, that window narrows, which is the main risk to Conviction's franchise.

insights.claim: Sarah raised fund one without a differentiated funnel story — offering a two-pager on her background, a claim to identify and support extraordinary people, and a promise to execute like hell and figure it out — and some LPs explicitly disliked the absence of a clean narrative.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A live counterexample to the LP orthodoxy that emerging managers need a fully specified strategy; the LPs who underwrote execution over story got the best-performing allocation.
insights.quote: She's going to execute like hell. We'll find out.

insights.claim: Sarah's fundraising principle, which she also gives founders, is to understand people's objections and questions but never to tell them what they want to hear, because you don't know your strategy until you make contact with reality.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Reframes the pitch as an honest-signal problem — telling a cleaner story than you believe buys capital but selects for the wrong partners.
insights.quote: you should understand people's objections to what you are doing and their questions but you should not tell them what they want to hear

insights.claim: Asked how many of her portfolio companies would not have been funded without her participation, Sarah estimates only 5-10% at most, since resourceful talented founders find other investors — though her presence may have unlocked the next hundred million dollars of compute.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: An unusually candid bound on investor value-add: the marginal contribution is not access to the round but access to the next tranche of compute capital.
insights.quote: couple of them 5% 10% max like they're resourceful really talented people they find other investors

insights.claim: Sarah rejects the zero-sum posture of traditional Series A/B firms that demand 18-25% ownership plus the board seat, arguing it is not conducive to collaboration, and prefers the public-markets norm of sharing best ideas so others pile in.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A structural competitive stance: positive-sum co-investment behavior as a sourcing advantage against ownership-maximizing incumbents in a market where allocation is the scarce good.
insights.quote: I'm going to own 18 to 25% of this company and take the board and you're going to own none of it

insights.claim: Sarah's risk-taking framework is to find the truth independent of dominant period narratives, identify where it is wrongly priced, and hold the position until others come around — asymmetric information plus protection from noise, not contrarianism for its own sake.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Distinguishes information edge from posture edge; only the former survives when the crowd is also positioned against consensus.
insights.quote: You want asymmetric information and then the confidence to like hold the opinion when other people haven't come around to it yet

insights.claim: Sarah names the firm's information sources as three distinct categories — portfolio founders, outside founders doing something surprising or advancing a frontier, and smart people who believe something she doesn't — and rates circular debate about big-lab strategy as not instructive for decision-making.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A concrete sourcing taxonomy for research process; note that the discourse most investors consume (lab strategy speculation) is explicitly excluded as low-value.

insights.claim: Sarah pushes back hard on the post-Gen-Z view that entrepreneurship reduces to marketing, brand, network and nepotism, arguing that focusing on value, treating people well and working with extraordinary people works more often than people expect.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A read on founder-selection: cynicism about the game is itself a negative signal in a founder, since the operators she cites win by customer obsession rather than positioning.

insights.claim: Sarah's central prediction for the next year is Jevons paradox in practice: agents and products handling the mundane across every domain, reproducing in other functions the speed transformation already visible in software engineering.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: The transferable template for forecasting AI adoption by function: look for where the software-engineering speedup pattern is starting, then assume it generalizes.
insights.quote: I'm hopeful that a year from now we see we see Jeban's paradox in practice

insights.claim: At one Conviction portfolio company serving many customers, the entire marketing department is one person in a house who built himself an autonomous marketing department to handle traditional work like sales enablement content.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: A live existence proof of headcount-free functional scaling — bearish for seat-based SaaS pricing in the functions being collapsed, bullish for agent tooling.
insights.quote: I made I made an autonomous marketing department for us the company

insights.claim: Asked whether AI has let her work less, Sarah says she works more — the productivity gain is being repurposed into more output rather than into leisure.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Direct anecdotal support for the Jevons interpretation of AI at work: demand for output expands to absorb the efficiency gain.
insights.quote: Yeah, I work more.

insights.claim: Sarah endorses Jensen's view that AI leaves everyone more employed rather than less, but conditions it on people being given access and education to the tooling that makes that possible.
insights.speaker: Sarah, founder of Conviction
insights.so_what: Frames the employment outcome as access-dependent, which is also the political variable that determines whether the anti-AI backlash scenario materializes.
insights.quote: we're all we're all going to be more employed
